Training item: Requesting — make him ask for what he wants
Exactly what to do (with example): Put a wanted item in sight but out of reach (iPad, chips, a toy). Hold it, look at him expectantly, and wait for him to ask before giving it. Example: he reaches for the iPad — you hold it and wait; when he says 'iPad' (or presses it on AAC), hand it over right away. Do this with at least 5 wanted items across the day.

When he makes a SHORT request, pause ~3-5 seconds with an expectant look instead of responding, so he upgrades it himself. Example: he says 'chips' — you pause and look at him; he adds 'I want chips' — then you give it. If he stays stuck after the pause, model 'I want chips' once and give it.

Training item: Honour the attempt, then model it back fuller
Exactly what to do (with example): Always give him the thing when he communicates, even if the word is imperfect — then repeat it back clearer/longer as you hand it over, with NO demand to repeat. Example: he says 'tv' but means iPad — hand him the iPad and say 'iPad — here's the iPad.' Or he says 'car' — give it and say 'yes, the red car.'

Model on his device at least a few times today: press the button as you say the word, during a real moment. Example: at snack time, press 'eat' and say 'eat' before giving food; at iPad time press 'iPad'. Accept either speech OR a button press as a successful request.

Sort or name things by colour during play, and work on adding ONE new colour (e.g. yellow). Example: put red and blue blocks in two piles and say 'give me the BLUE one'; or at snack, 'point to the red apple.' Reward correct tries with a bite or a turn.

Count real objects out loud together, pointing to each one. Example: count his crackers before he eats them ('1, 2, 3... 16'), or count stairs as you climb. Let him say the numbers he can and you fill the rest.
Find and name numbers on real things. Example: 'find number 3' on the TV remote, on a door, or on number cards; match two cards with the same number. Keep it a quick game.
Give a clear two-part instruction and help only if needed. Example: 'Get your shoes AND bring them to me,' or 'Pick up the cup and put it in the sink.' As he succeeds, try adding a third step.

Trace dotted lines, shapes, and zigzags with a thick crayon or marker. Example: print or draw dotted horizontal, vertical and zigzag lines and have him trace over them; make it a 'follow the road' game.

Have him trace then copy numbers 1-5, giving LESS hand help over time. Example: today guide his hand lightly for '3'; next time just start the stroke; aim for him doing it alone. Note how much help he needed.
Any hand-control activity. Example: colour inside a big simple shape, do a simple maze, or play with play-dough, stickers, threading beads, or opening/closing containers.
Practise during normal dressing, offering less help each time. Example: start the sock over his toes and let him pull it up; next time let him start it. Note the help level.

Let him brush, then take a quick 'my turn' to reach both sides. Example: he brushes, then you say 'my turn!' and brush the back/sides; or use a 2-minute timer or mirror game so he brushes longer and everywhere.

Play a back-and-forth game that builds waiting. Example: roll a ball back and forth saying 'my turn... your turn'; or stack blocks one each; or a short wait with a count ('wait — 1, 2, 3 — okay!') before giving something.

Training item: End on a success + catch him being good
Exactly what to do (with example): Finish each session with something he can do and enjoys, and praise/reward the moments he tries, waits, or stays with a task. Example: end a hard counting session with one easy count he nails, then 'great counting!' and a chip or a turn on the iPad.

Watch a language-building show WITH him and make it interactive — pause when it pauses, model the word, encourage him to say or sign it. Example: watch Ms Rachel; when she pauses for a word, you say it and wait for him to try; cheer any attempt. A few engaged minutes beat a long passive stretch.
